newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB sees Canadian 1997/98 barley production lower.
newsitem.headline: CWB sees Canadian 1997/98 barley production lower.

text.p: Canadian barley production in 1997 is expected to decline about three million tonnes to 15.9 million tonnes due to acreage switching back to canola, Canadian Wheat Board marketing manager Ramzy Yelda said.

In an outlook presented at the CWB's annual Grain World conference, Yelda said production is also expected to fall in Australia and the United States. But a large rise in European Union supplies should keep a lid on prices, he said.
CWB earlier released its first Pool Return Outlook price projections for the 1997/98 (Aug/July) year, with feed barley seen at C$110-140 per tonne versus $143-158 a year earlier.

Yelda said 1997/98 world barley carry-in stocks would rise an estimated 8 million tonnes to 26 million tonnes. World production should remain basically unchanged at 158 million tonnes and usage rise 5 million to 155 million, leaving carry-out stocks at the end of 1997/98 at 28.7 million tonnes.

Australian and U.S. 1997/98 production were projected to fall about 500,000 tonnes each in 1997/98 to 6.1 million and 8.6 million tonnes, respectively. EU output is seen slightly snaller than last season's 53.6 million tonnes. But EU barley stocks are nevertheless expected to double to 10 million tonnes by June 1997 after 1995/96 production rose 23 percent.

"The EU Commission will be under pressure to ensure a large export program projected at over 8 million tonnes (including malt) in 1997/98, compared with 7 million tonnes in the current year and 4.1 million tonnes in 1995/96," he said.
Yelda said Europe would continue subsidizing barley exports including malting barley, where subsidies should be "aggressive" for projected world demand of 3.5 million tonnes.

"The EU will probably maintain large export refunds but it is expected to behave in a relatively disciplined fashion, i.e. export subsidies will probably not fluctuate drastically over short periods of time," Yelda said.

Yelda said that on the demand side, imports of feed barley by Saudi Arabia and malting barley by China were expected to stay very strong, with 1997/98 imports by each close to the current season's projected purchases of 5.5 million tonnes by Saudi Arabia and 1.5 million tonnes by China.
U.S. maltsters have become more familiar at using barley tainted with vomitoxin, so the premium for negative DON (or vomitoxin-free grain) has fallen this year, Yelda said.
"However, each crop performs differently and fusarium is a problem that is expected to affect U.S. six-row barley for a number of years," he said.

"After the usual new-crop inverse, we expect barley prices to stabilize," Yelda said, with malting barley expected to maintain a healthy premium to feed barley and with two-row varieties trading at a premium to six-row varieties.

CWB earlier projected CW two-row designated barley prices at $165-195 a tonne in its first 1997/98 Pool Return Outlook, against $223-233 a year earlier. The six-row barley was pegged at $130-160 a tonne, against $186-196.

Weather remains the key factor, Yelda said. Last year's winterkill in the EU caused significant reseeding with spring barley, resulting in a higher percentage of malting barley. This year, lack of winterkill means the EU should return to a more normal percentage of malting barley production, he said.
